frmcs.title: FRMCS: the new 5G rail radio
frmcs.lede: GSM-R has been Europe's digital train radio since the 2000s and is based on 2G. Its successor FRMCS (Future Railway Mobile Communication System) brings 5G to the railway. We help infrastructure managers, rolling stock manufacturers and suppliers prepare the migration technically.
frmcs.teaser: Migration from GSM-R to FRMCS: radio planning in n100 and n101, coexistence, on-board integration and test concepts.

sections.title: Why GSM-R is being replaced
paras: GSM-R runs on roughly 130,000 km of line in Europe. The technology comes from the 2G era, suppliers and spare parts are getting scarce, and the bandwidth is too low for new data applications such as automatic train operation (ATO), video or vehicle diagnostics.
The European Union Agency for Railways (ERA) expects GSM-R to become unsustainable between 2035 and 2040. By then, lines and vehicles have to be migrated while trains keep running.

sections.title: What FRMCS is technically
paras: FRMCS is a 5G standalone network. On top of it run the 3GPP mission-critical services: MCPTT for voice group and emergency calls, MCData for data applications. The railway requirements come from the International Union of Railways (UIC); the technical specifications are written by ETSI committee TC RT and 3GPP.

On the train, the Telecom On-Board Architecture (TOBA) provides radio access for all on-board applications. ETCS and ATO connect through a standardised interface (OBapp), so signalling and radio suppliers can already develop their equipment against a common interface.

sections.title: The spectrum
paras: With Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/1730, the EU harmonised two ranges for railway radio: the paired 900 MHz band (874.4–880 MHz and 919.4–925 MHz, 3GPP band n100) and the unpaired 1900 MHz band (1900–1910 MHz, band n101).

Both bands are narrow. The 900 MHz band offers only 5.6 MHz per direction, and GSM-R shares it during the transition. The 1900 MHz band adds capacity but, with higher path loss, needs a denser network. On-board equipment has to switch between both bands while the train is moving.

sections.title: The timeline
paras: Regulation (EU) 2023/1695 (CCS TSI 2023) added FRMCS to the European framework for the first time, but only partially: what is fixed is mainly the interface between ETCS/ATO and the FRMCS on-board unit. According to ERA, that is not yet enough to tender on-board equipment.

The first complete, tender-ready version (FRMCS 1st Edition, V3) is due with the next TSI revision, currently expected in 2027 or 2028. In the EU project MORANE-2, laboratory testing has been running since 2026. Field tests with several railways, including DB InfraGO in Germany, follow from 2027.

Deutsche Bahn expects GSM-R to remain in use for at least another ten years. As part of its general refurbishment, the Hamburg–Berlin line has already been prepared with fibre and masts for a first FRMCS trial operation.

sections.title: The engineering questions of the migration
paras: Between today and regular operation lie questions that specifications alone do not answer:
bullets: Coexistence and interworking with GSM-R over many years, on the same lines and partly in the same frequencies
Robustness against public mobile networks transmitting just above 925 MHz, a problem GSM-R already knows
Radio planning along the line for 900 and 1900 MHz, including which existing sites can be reused
On-board integration: antennas, roof space, coexistence with other radio systems on the vehicle
Test concepts that grow with specification versions V1, V2 and V3 instead of starting over with every revision

contribution: Technical assessment and migration concepts: what does FRMCS mean for your lines, vehicles or products, and in which order?
Radio planning and coexistence analyses for n100 and n101, including interference scenarios with public networks
Architecture and integration of the 5G standalone core and mission-critical services, as we know them from private 5G projects
Requirements management, test concepts and test campaigns along the specification versions

kritis.title: KRITIS and NIS2: what Germany's new obligations mean for your networks
kritis.lede: Germany's NIS2 Implementation Act has applied since December 2025, the KRITIS umbrella act since March 2026. Both require far more companies than before to protect their IT and facilities against outages and attacks, and radio, mobile and campus networks are part of that. This page covers the German and EU framework; in the US and Brazil different rules apply, which we assess project by project.
kritis.teaser: Technical implementation of NIS2 and KRITIS obligations for radio, mobile and campus networks.

sections.title: Two laws, two kinds of protection
paras: The NIS2 Implementation Act (NIS2UmsuCG) transposes the EU NIS2 Directive and rewrote Germany's BSI Act. It is about cybersecurity: risk management, incident reporting and management accountability. It has applied since 6 December 2025, without a transition period.

The KRITIS umbrella act (KRITIS-Dachgesetz) transposes the EU CER Directive and covers the physical resilience of critical facilities, meaning protection against natural hazards, sabotage or power failure. It has applied since 17 March 2026. Which facilities count as critical is set out in a separate ordinance, and operators' deadlines only start once a facility has been classified.

sections.title: Who is affected
paras: NIS2 distinguishes two groups. Essential entities are operators of critical facilities, regardless of size, plus large companies in highly critical sectors (from 250 employees, or more than €50m turnover and more than €43m balance sheet total). Important entities are usually medium-sized companies from 50 employees or more than €10m turnover and balance sheet total.

Operators of public telecommunications networks and providers of public telecommunications services count as essential from medium size onwards. In rail, infrastructure managers and railway undertakings are covered. The BSI expects around 29,500 companies and institutions in total. By the end of June 2026, around 17,700 had registered.

sections.title: Obligations under NIS2
bullets: Registration with the BSI no later than three months after a company first falls under the law
Reporting of significant incidents: early warning within 24 hours, notification within 72 hours, final report after 30 days
Risk management covering at least ten areas, including risk analysis, incident handling, business continuity, supply-chain security, cryptography and multi-factor authentication
Management must implement and oversee the measures, attend regular training and is liable for culpable breaches
Fines of up to €10m or 2 % of worldwide turnover (essential entities) or up to €7m or 1.4 % (important entities)

sections.title: Obligations under the KRITIS umbrella act
paras: Operators of critical facilities also face physical-resilience obligations. Deadlines run from the facility's classification as critical:
bullets: Registration on the joint BBK and BSI platform within three months
Risk assessment within nine months
Resilience measures and a resilience plan within ten months
Incident reporting within 24 hours
after: The standard threshold is a supply of 500,000 inhabitants. For rail, the Federal Railway Authority (Eisenbahn-Bundesamt) is responsible.

sections.title: What this means for radio and campus networks
paras: A purely internal campus network is usually not a public telecommunications network, so the specific security duties of the German Telecommunications Act (sections 165 ff. TKG) mostly do not apply directly. If the company falls under NIS2 or operates a critical facility, however, the network is part of the IT systems that risk management under section 30 BSIG must cover. Whether this applies in a given case should be checked legally.

Supplier choice is becoming more important too. Under section 41 BSIG, the Federal Ministry of the Interior can prohibit operators of critical facilities from using a manufacturer's critical components. Germany's large mobile network operators have contractually committed to the federal government to remove critical Huawei and ZTE components from their 5G core networks by the end of 2026.

contribution: Inventory of your radio, mobile and campus networks: which systems are critical to operations, and where are single points of failure?
Network architecture with redundancy, segmentation and secured transitions to the rest of your IT
Supplier and component assessment as input to supply-chain security
Technical concepts for monitoring, detection and incident reporting paths
Technical input for your risk analysis and resilience plan
kritis.limits: We are an engineering consultancy, not a law firm and not an audit body. Your lawyers clarify whether and how your company is affected, and accredited bodies provide audits and evidence. We deliver the technical basis and work with both.
kritis.asOf: As of October 2026. This page is a technical overview, not legal advice.

fieldNotes.title: Measure first, then plan.
fieldNotes.text: Datasheets and simulations are a start. How radio really behaves in a building or on a site only shows up in on-site measurements. That is why we measure at the beginning, not at the end.

fieldNotes.title: The technology is rarely the problem.
fieldNotes.text: More often things stall at the handovers: between IT and operations, between several suppliers, between requirements and tender. We sort out these points early, before they cost time and money.

fieldNotes.title: Someone has to be able to run the network.
fieldNotes.text: The best design does little good if nobody knows how it works after handover. We document it so that your team understands the network and can develop it further on its own.

esim.title: eSIM and iSIM: SIM profiles you can change remotely
esim.lede: An eSIM is no longer a card but a chip onto which mobile network profiles are loaded over the air. For IoT devices that run for ten or fifteen years, that decides whether you can still switch operators later. We plan the eSIM architecture from manufacturing to profile changes in the field.
esim.teaser: eSIM and iSIM architecture to GSMA SGP.32: profile management, manufacturing, lifecycle and security.

sections.title: What eSIM and iSIM actually are
paras: The eUICC is the secure chip that can store several operator profiles: download, enable, disable, delete. eSIM usually refers to exactly this remote provisioning (Remote SIM Provisioning), sometimes to the soldered MFF2 form factor.

With iSIM, the eUICC is no longer a separate component on the board but sits in a protected security area of the system-on-chip. That saves space and cost. The GSMA requires a separately certified security area for it.

sections.title: SGP.32: the eSIM for IoT
paras: Smartphones have used SGP.22 for years. It fitted IoT devices poorly: there is often no screen for anyone to confirm a profile change, and little bandwidth. The older M2M variant, SGP.02, was complex to integrate.

SGP.31/32 closes this gap with two new components: the eIM, a server that controls the profiles of an entire device fleet, and the IPA, which sits in the device or directly in the eUICC. The current version V1.3 was published in May 2026, and the first manufacturers have reported certified SGP.32 products since 2025.

sections.title: Profiles from the factory and for fifteen years
paras: Since 2025, SGP.41 describes how profiles can be loaded onto the eUICC in the device factory, for soldered eUICCs as well as for iSIM. The corresponding technical specification is still pending.

In the field, the lifecycle is what counts: a meter or machine controller often runs longer than any mobile contract. If profile changes are not planned from day one, you stay tied to the first provider.

sections.title: Where regulation has a say
paras: Not every country allows devices to run permanently on a foreign profile in roaming:
bullets: Turkey: the regulator BTK has limited roaming of imported eSIM devices to 120 days since 2019.
Brazil: Anatel treats roaming beyond 90 days as permanent and objected to such an M2M offer in 2022.
after: For these markets the device needs a local profile, and the architecture has to be able to switch to it.

sections.title: The engineering questions
paras: Before the first component is ordered, we clarify with you:
bullets: Are hardware and software designed for SGP.32, or do legacy devices still depend on SGP.02, and what is the migration path?
Who operates the eIM, and how does a later change of eIM and network operator remain technically and contractually possible?
Which profile goes onto the device in the factory, and how is manufacturing connected?
In which countries does the device run permanently, and where is a local profile mandatory?
Soldered eUICC or iSIM: space, energy, availability of module and chipset, certification status

contribution: eSIM architecture to SGP.32: eIM, IPA, profile strategy and provider selection
Integration into manufacturing and logistics, from the first profile to commissioning
Lifecycle concept for profile changes in the field, including the energy budget on NB-IoT and LTE-M

iot.title: IoT connectivity: many devices, little data, long lifetimes
iot.lede: Meters, sensors and trackers send rarely and little, but they have to run on one battery for years and still have coverage in the basement. NB-IoT, LTE-M and RedCap provide the right mobile technology for this. We help you choose and plan the migration away from 2G.
iot.teaser: Connectivity for massive IoT: NB-IoT, LTE-M and RedCap, energy budget, coverage and 2G migration.

sections.title: NB-IoT or LTE-M?
paras: Both technologies come from 3GPP Release 13 and, under the ITU requirements, count as part of 5G for massive machine-type communication. NB-IoT is very narrowband, needs little energy and reaches deep into buildings: with coverage enhancement levels the permissible coupling loss rises to up to 164 dB, at the cost of energy consumption.
LTE-M uses 1.4 MHz of bandwidth, offers higher data rates and full mobility. That suits trackers and mobile devices. Voice would be technically possible but is rarely offered by operators.

sections.title: The energy budget
paras: With Power Saving Mode and eDRX, a device sleeps most of the time and wakes only for short transmission windows. The GSMA cites up to ten years of battery life this way, depending on the data profile.

The device only requests the timers, though; the network decides. And a poorly configured connection in the backend can wipe out the savings. That is why we calculate the energy budget against real network behaviour, not just the datasheet.

sections.title: 2G sunset: the timeline is set
paras: 3G was switched off in Germany in 2021. For 2G, operators have announced their dates: Telekom expected on 30 June 2028, Vodafone in September 2028 with exceptions for critical IoT until the end of 2030, Telefónica at the end of 2028.
Anyone still running meters, alarm systems or telematics on 2G now has a fixed deadline. For long-lived devices, the successor technology should be planned now.

sections.title: RedCap and satellite
paras: For applications between IoT sensor and smartphone, such as cameras, wearables or industrial sensors with more data, Release 17 introduced RedCap: 5G with up to 20 MHz of bandwidth and simplified hardware. Release 18 adds eRedCap for even lower-cost devices.
Where mobile networks do not reach, NB-IoT and LTE-M can also run over satellite since Release 17. More on our page on non-terrestrial networks.

sections.title: The engineering questions
paras: For a sound technology choice, we clarify with you:
bullets: Which devices still run on 2G, what has to be migrated by 2028, and to what?
What does the data profile look like: message size, frequency, commands to the device, maximum latency?
Where is the device installed, in a basement, a meter cabinet, a metal housing, and which coverage level does that need?
Does the device move, does it need roaming, and does the module support the required bands?
Which module and chipset will be available for the whole product lifetime, and should an SGP.32 eSIM be designed in right away?

ntn.title: Non-terrestrial networks: mobile connectivity via satellite
ntn.lede: Since 3GPP Release 17, satellites are part of the mobile standard. Devices can use the same technology via a cell tower and via satellite, for regions without coverage, for ships, pipelines or as a fallback for critical facilities. We assess where that works and how satellite and terrestrial networks play together.
ntn.teaser: Satellite 5G to 3GPP: orbit choice, link budget, hybrid operation with the terrestrial network and resilience.

facts.v: GEO approx. 540 ms · LEO 600 km approx. 26 ms

sections.title: What 3GPP has standardised
paras: Release 17 set the first binding rules for NTN in 2022, both for 5G NR and for NB-IoT and LTE-M via satellite. The device knows its position via GNSS and compensates delay and Doppler shift itself, using orbit data the network broadcasts in every cell.

Release 18 improved uplink coverage and mobility between satellite and terrestrial networks. Release 19 has been ready for implementation since the end of 2025 and adds, among other things, satellites that run 5G functions on board and store-and-forward for IoT.

sections.title: Orbit, delay, link budget
paras: According to the reference values of the 3GPP study, a packet takes around 540 ms round trip via a geostationary satellite and around 26 ms via a low-earth-orbit satellite at 600 km. LEO satellites, however, move quickly across the sky, which means constant handovers and strong Doppler.

What decides the use case is the link budget: a smartphone with a small antenna needs a clear view of the sky and gets by with low data rates. The Ka-band is intended for fixed terminals with directional antennas.

sections.title: Satellite direct to device
paras: The first services are live: emergency messaging via satellite is available on current iPhones in 21 countries, including Germany, and a Release 17 NB-IoT satellite service has been commercially available in North America since 2024.

In Europe, the EU is currently reorganising the 2 GHz band for mobile satellite services because today's licences expire in 2027. With IRIS², the EU is also building its own system of 348 satellites for public authorities and emergency services, with first launches planned for 2029.

sections.title: Satellite as a fallback
paras: For operators of critical infrastructure, NTN is above all a second, independent connection: if the mobile network or fibre fails, telemetry and alarms continue via satellite. That requires failover, data prioritisation and billing to be planned in advance.

sections.title: The engineering questions
paras: Before a satellite provider is selected, we clarify with you:
bullets: Which orbit and architecture fit latency, availability and budget?
Is the link budget sufficient for the planned device, with antenna, transmit power and installation site?
How are satellite and terrestrial network connected: roaming, failover, prioritisation?
What data volumes are expected, and what does that mean for running costs?
What spectrum and licensing rules apply at the site?

sixg.title: 6G: what is settled and what you can prepare today
sixg.lede: According to today's plan, 6G arrives around 2030. The cornerstones are in place: the ITU has set the framework, 3GPP is working on the first studies, and candidate bands will be discussed in 2027. We advise on which decisions made today will still hold in a 6G network.
sixg.teaser: 6G readiness along ITU IMT-2030 and 3GPP Rel-20/21: timeline, spectrum and future-proof architecture.

sections.title: The timeline
paras: With IMT-2030, the ITU set the framework for 6G in November 2023. Candidate technologies can be submitted between February 2027 and February 2029. At 3GPP, the first 6G studies are running in Release 20; the actual standard is created in Release 21 and is due to be completed in 2029.
First commercial networks are expected around 2030. For investments made today, that means they will almost certainly still be running when 6G arrives.

sections.title: What 6G is meant to do
paras: The ITU describes six usage scenarios. Besides the familiar ones from 5G, three are new:
bullets: Integrated sensing and communication: the network detects objects and movement, not just devices
Artificial intelligence and communication: AI in the network and networks for AI applications
Ubiquitous connectivity, including via satellite
after: The ITU names target ranges such as peak rates of 50 to 200 Gbit/s and positioning to within one to ten centimetres. These are goals from the framework document, not promised values.

sections.title: New spectrum
paras: For the World Radiocommunication Conference 2027, three ranges are being studied for mobile: 4.4 to 4.8 GHz, 7.125 to 8.4 GHz and 14.8 to 15.35 GHz. The range around 7 GHz in particular is seen as a 6G candidate because it combines capacity and reach.

sections.title: What you can prepare today
paras: Following the first fundamental decisions at 3GPP, 6G is to start as a standalone system and share spectrum dynamically with 5G. Our assessment: anyone deploying 5G standalone with a cloud-native core today is building on the architecture 6G will connect to. Exactly how the core transition will work is still being decided at 3GPP.

sections.title: The engineering questions
paras: For future-proof planning, we clarify with you:
bullets: Is today's core network 5G standalone capable and cloud-native, or is the older architecture still in use?
Which components can be upgraded by software, and which hardware will be written off by 2030 anyway?
Which spectrum is in use today, and what does the 7 GHz band mean for sites and antennas?
Which applications really need 6G capabilities, and which can already be solved with 5G-Advanced?

platform.title: Connectivity platforms: SIMs, networks and data under control
platform.lede: Anyone operating thousands of connected devices in several countries needs an overview: which SIM is active, what it consumes, where a connection drops. Connectivity management platforms and open network interfaces exist for exactly this. We plan the architecture so that you do not depend on a single provider.
platform.teaser: Connectivity management, open network APIs (CAMARA, Open Gateway) and telemetry with MQTT and LwM2M.

facts.v: Quality on Demand · Device Location · SIM Swap

sections.title: What a connectivity platform does
paras: A connectivity management platform manages the SIM cards of a device fleet across their whole lifecycle: zero-touch activation, rate plans, usage data, diagnostics, alerts on anomalies and increasingly remote management of eSIM profiles. Network operators offer such platforms to their business customers.
The catch: every platform belongs to one provider. Anyone using several networks or countries quickly ends up with several interfaces and data formats.

sections.title: Open network interfaces
paras: With Open Gateway, the GSMA launched a joint operator initiative in 2023 to offer network functions through uniform interfaces. By early 2026, more than 85 operator groups were involved. The interfaces themselves are defined in the Linux Foundation's open-source project CAMARA.
bullets: Quality on Demand: better quality of service for a connection on request
Device Location: location verification via the network
SIM Swap: an indication of whether a SIM was recently swapped, useful against fraud
after: An open standard does not mean every operator offers every interface, though. That has to be checked market by market.

sections.title: Telemetry and device management
paras: For data transport, MQTT has become the norm, an OASIS standard in version 5.0 since 2019. For managing the devices themselves, meaning configuration, firmware and status data, there is LwM2M from OMA SpecWorks, currently in version 1.2.2. Both are open and vendor-independent.

sections.title: Staying independent
paras: Combining a platform with open network interfaces, open protocols and SGP.32 eSIM lets you switch network operator and platform later without touching the devices in the field. That is the real architecture decision, not the choice of user interface.

sections.title: The engineering questions
paras: For the platform architecture, we clarify with you:
bullets: How many networks, providers and countries have to be covered, and is a single provider platform enough?
Where do usage, location and device data reside, and what is the legal basis under GDPR?
Which interfaces are needed to connect ERP, billing and IoT platform?
Which CAMARA interfaces do the chosen operators actually offer?
How do data stay exportable and a change of provider possible?
